parts.title: 大問1 短文の語句空所補充
parts.desc: 1〜2文・会話の空所に入る単語・句動詞を4つから選ぶ（準1級の語彙）
parts.tip: まず空所の後ろの2文目や because / but / despite を見て「良い意味か悪い意味か」を決める。次に前置詞（convert A into B, susceptible to）で形を絞る。句動詞は動詞より後ろの小さい語（down / out / up）の意味をつかむ。
parts.intro: Read each sentence or short exchange and choose the word or phrase that best fills the blank.

questions.q: The committee voted to ____ the outdated rule after several members complained that it no longer served any useful purpose and only slowed down decision-making.
choices: inhabit
endorse
provoke
abolish
questions.why: abolish＝「（制度・規則を）廃止する」。役に立たず決定を遅らせるだけ、という理由に合う。inhabit（住む）、endorse（支持する）、provoke（引き起こす）は理由と合わない。

questions.q: Despite the ____ weather forecast, thousands of fans gathered in the park for the outdoor concert, and fortunately the rain held off until the final song.
choices: lavish
gloomy
fragile
vacant
questions.why: gloomy＝「（天気・見通しが）暗い、悪い」。Despite と「幸い雨は最後まで降らなかった」から、予報は悪かったと分かる。lavish（豪華な）、fragile（壊れやすい）、vacant（空いている）は予報に合わない。

questions.q: The professor's lecture was so ____ that many students struggled to follow it. She kept jumping from topic to topic without explaining how they were connected.
choices: concise
punctual
incoherent
unanimous
questions.why: incoherent＝「まとまりのない、筋の通らない」。話題が飛び、つながりを説明しない、が根拠。concise（簡潔な）は逆の意味。punctual（時間を守る）、unanimous（満場一致の）は講義の説明にならない。

questions.q: After months of difficult negotiations, the two companies finally reached a ____, with each side agreeing to give up some of its original demands.
choices: deficit
monopoly
compromise
surplus
questions.why: reach a compromise＝「妥協に至る」。お互いに要求の一部をあきらめた、が妥協の中身。deficit（赤字）、monopoly（独占）、surplus（黒字・余剰）は交渉の結果として合わない。

questions.q: The hikers were forced to ____ their attempt to reach the summit when a thick fog rolled in and made the narrow path too dangerous to follow.
choices: enforce
abort
simulate
inherit
questions.why: abort＝「（途中で）中止する」。霧で道が危険になり、登頂の試みをやめた。enforce（施行する）、simulate（模擬実験する）、inherit（受け継ぐ）は were forced to と合わない。

questions.q: Jenna is extremely ____ about her work. She checks every report three times before submitting it, so her manager almost never finds any mistakes.
choices: reluctant
hostile
meticulous
indifferent
questions.why: meticulous＝「細心の、きちょうめんな」。3回確認する・ミスがほぼ無い、が具体例。indifferent（無関心な）は逆。reluctant（気が進まない）、hostile（敵意のある）も例と合わない。

questions.q: The new medicine can ____ the symptoms of the illness, but it cannot actually cure it, so patients still need to have regular checkups.
choices: alleviate
dictate
confiscate
fabricate
questions.why: alleviate＝「（苦痛・症状を）和らげる」。but で「治すことはできない」と続くので、症状を軽くする意味が入る。dictate（命じる）、confiscate（没収する）、fabricate（でっち上げる）は症状に使わない。

questions.q: Many residents were ____ of the developer's promises, as the same company had failed to complete a similar project in the neighboring town.
choices: fond
ashamed
envious
skeptical
questions.why: be skeptical of ～＝「～を疑っている」。隣町で同じ会社が計画を終えられなかった、が疑う理由。fond of（好きだ）、ashamed of（恥じる）、envious of（うらやむ）は理由とつながらない。

questions.q:
A: I can't believe how much the price of coffee has gone up this year.
B: I know. Experts say it's because of a ____ of beans caused by poor harvests in several countries.
choices: scarcity
fraction
venue
hazard
questions.why: scarcity＝「不足、欠乏」。不作で豆が足りず値上がりした、という因果。fraction（一部分）、venue（会場）、hazard（危険）では値上がりの理由にならない。

questions.q: The author's latest novel received ____ praise from critics, who all agreed that it was the finest book she had ever written.
choices: tentative
obsolete
sluggish
unanimous
questions.why: unanimous＝「満場一致の」。批評家が全員（all agreed）最高傑作と認めた。tentative（仮の・ためらいがちな）は all agreed と合わない。obsolete（時代遅れの）、sluggish（のろい）も不可。

questions.q: The city council plans to ____ the old textile factory into a community center with a library, a gym, and studios for local artists.
choices: deprive
exempt
dissuade
convert
questions.why: convert A into B＝「AをBに改造する」。into と組むのは convert。deprive A of B（奪う）、exempt A from B（免除する）、dissuade A from ～ing（思いとどまらせる）は前置詞も意味も合わない。

questions.q: The small family bakery has managed to ____ despite strong competition from supermarket chains, mainly because customers love its traditional recipes.
choices: thrive
dwindle
falter
recede
questions.why: thrive＝「繁盛する」。despite（競争にもかかわらず）と「客に愛されている」から、うまくいっている意味。dwindle（だんだん減る）、falter（ぐらつく）、recede（後退する）は逆の流れ。

questions.q: Because the assembly instructions were so ____, many customers put the bookshelf together incorrectly and had to call the company for help.
choices: ambiguous
generous
authentic
vigorous
questions.why: ambiguous＝「あいまいな、2通りに取れる」。説明書のせいで組み立てを間違えた、という結果から。generous（気前のよい）、authentic（本物の）、vigorous（活発な）は説明書の欠点にならない。

questions.q: The athlete's ____ to recover from a serious knee injury and win a gold medal two years later inspired many young people across the country.
choices: hesitation
imitation
consumption
determination
questions.why: determination to do＝「～しようという固い決意」。大けがから立ち直り金メダル、が人々を励ました。hesitation（ためらい）は逆。imitation（模倣）、consumption（消費）は意味が通らない。

questions.q: Tom tried to ____ his disappointment when he was not chosen for the promotion, but his colleagues could tell from his face that he was upset.
choices: conceal
nominate
assemble
cultivate
questions.why: conceal＝「隠す」。but で「顔を見れば分かった」と続くので、隠そうとした。nominate（指名する）、assemble（組み立てる）、cultivate（耕す・育てる）は失望に使わない。

questions.q: Online reviews can have a ____ effect on small restaurants. Just a few negative comments may be enough to drive customers away for months.
choices: nominal
cordial
profound
redundant
questions.why: profound effect＝「大きな影響」。数件の悪い口コミで何か月も客が離れる、が影響の大きさ。nominal（名ばかりの・わずかな）は逆。cordial（心からの）、redundant（余分な）も合わない。

questions.q: Visitors are not allowed to touch the artworks in the museum, as even small amounts of oil from human skin can ____ the surface of old paintings.
choices: reinforce
degrade
illuminate
replicate
questions.why: degrade＝「劣化させる」。触ってはいけない理由なので、悪い影響を表す語。reinforce（補強する）、illuminate（照らす）、replicate（複製する）は禁止の理由にならない。

questions.q: After the merger, several senior managers ____ from the company because they strongly disagreed with the new owner's plans for the business.
choices: inquired
resigned
collided
emerged
questions.why: resign from ～＝「～を辞職する」。新しい経営者の方針に反対だった、が理由。inquired（尋ねた）、collided（衝突した）、emerged（現れた）は from the company と組んでも意味を成さない。

questions.q: Scientists warn that if fish populations continue to ____ at the current rate, many coastal communities could lose their main source of income.
choices: flourish
linger
dwindle
prevail
questions.why: dwindle＝「だんだん減る」。魚が減れば漁村が収入を失う、という警告。flourish（栄える）では収入を失う理由にならない。linger（長引く）、prevail（広まる）も不可。

questions.q: The manager praised Kenji for his ____ response to the customer's complaint. He apologized immediately and offered a full refund within minutes.
choices: vague
dormant
prompt
brittle
questions.why: prompt＝「迅速な」。すぐ謝り数分で返金、が根拠。vague（あいまいな）、dormant（休止中の）、brittle（もろい）では褒める理由にならない。

questions.q: Although the twin sisters look almost ____, people who know them well can easily tell them apart by their voices and the way they laugh.
choices: incompatible
insistent
indispensable
indistinguishable
questions.why: indistinguishable＝「区別がつかない」。Although と tell them apart（見分ける）から、見た目はそっくりだと分かる。incompatible（相性が悪い）、insistent（しつこい）、indispensable（不可欠な）は形が似ているだけ。

questions.q: The documentary gives a ____ account of daily life in a remote mountain village, clearly showing both the joys and the hardships of the residents.
choices: frantic
reckless
vivid
stale
questions.why: vivid account＝「生き生きとした描写」。喜びも苦労もはっきり見せる、が根拠。frantic（取り乱した）、reckless（無謀な）、stale（新鮮でない）は良い描写の意味にならない。

questions.q: Visitors to the national park are reminded that feeding the wild animals is strictly ____ and can result in a heavy fine.
choices: inevitable
contagious
prohibited
negligible
questions.why: prohibited＝「禁止されている」。重い罰金になる、が根拠。inevitable（避けられない）、contagious（伝染性の）、negligible（ごくわずかな）は罰金と結びつかない。

questions.q: The new employee felt ____ at her first team meeting because she did not know anyone and was unsure whether she was allowed to speak.
choices: apprehensive
jubilant
lenient
spacious
questions.why: apprehensive＝「不安な、心配な」。知り合いがおらず発言してよいか分からない、が理由。jubilant（大喜びの）は逆。lenient（寛大な）、spacious（広々とした）は気持ちを表さない。

questions.q: Recent discoveries have ____ the long-held belief that dinosaurs were slow, cold-blooded creatures, showing that many of them were actually active and fast.
choices: endured
refuted
nurtured
embraced
questions.why: refute＝「（説を）誤りだと証明する」。実は活発で速かったと示した、が根拠。embraced（受け入れた）は逆。endured（耐えた）、nurtured（育てた）は説に使わない。

questions.q: The charity relies almost entirely on ____ from local businesses and individuals to fund the free meals it provides for elderly residents.
choices: allegations
contributions
restrictions
quarrels
questions.why: contribution＝「寄付」。無料の食事の資金を何に頼るか、なので寄付。allegations（申し立て）、restrictions（制限）、quarrels（口論）は資金にならない。

questions.q: The report criticized the company for its ____ use of plastic packaging, pointing out that most of it was unnecessary and could easily be replaced with paper.
choices: frugal
excessive
sparse
sincere
questions.why: excessive＝「過剰な」。ほとんどが不要だった、が批判の中身。frugal（倹約的な）、sparse（まばらな）は逆。sincere（誠実な）は批判と合わない。

questions.q:
A: Did you hear that the café on Pine Street is closing?
B: Yes. The owner said rising rent means the business is no longer financially ____, so she's moving to a cheaper area.
choices: viable
fluent
sedentary
impartial
questions.why: financially viable＝「経営的に成り立つ」。家賃が上がり続けられないので安い地域へ移る。fluent（流ちょうな）、sedentary（座りがちな）、impartial（公平な）は事業の状態を表さない。

questions.q: Many parents worry that children who spend several hours a day looking at screens may be more ____ to eye problems and poor sleep.
choices: obedient
adjacent
indebted
susceptible
questions.why: be susceptible to ～＝「～にかかりやすい」。画面を長く見る子は目の問題や睡眠不足になりやすい。obedient to（従順な）、adjacent to（隣接した）、indebted to（恩がある）は病気に使わない。

questions.q: The hotel staff went out of their way to ____ the guests' special requests, such as preparing a vegetarian breakfast and arranging an early check-in.
choices: contaminate
intimidate
deteriorate
accommodate
questions.why: accommodate a request＝「要望に応える」。菜食の朝食・早いチェックインの手配が具体例。contaminate（汚染する）、intimidate（おどす）、deteriorate（悪化する）は合わない。

questions.q: The company had to ____ its plans to open a new branch overseas after sales fell sharply in the first half of the year.
choices: hand down
scale back
phase in
fill out
questions.why: scale back＝「（計画を）縮小する」。売上の急落が理由。hand down（伝える）、phase in（段階的に導入する）、fill out（記入する）は売上が落ちた時の対応として合わない。

questions.q: When Martin lost his job last spring, several of his close friends ____ to help him pay his rent until he found new work.
choices: chipped in
stood out
pulled through
ran over
questions.why: chip in＝「（お金を）出し合う」。家賃を払う手助け、なのでお金を出し合った。stood out（目立った）、pulled through（切り抜けた）、ran over（ひいた・あふれた）は合わない。

questions.q: The talks between the two firms nearly ____ when neither side would accept the other's terms, but a last-minute offer saved the deal.
choices: took after
broke down
wore off
looked up
questions.why: break down＝「（交渉が）決裂する」。どちらも条件をのまず、最後の提案で救われた。took after（似ている）、wore off（薄れた）、looked up（良くなった）は交渉の危機を表さない。

questions.q: Lisa's idea of opening a bookstore with a café seemed risky at first, but it ____ well, and she now runs three shops in the city.
choices: backed down
dropped by
panned out
cut in
questions.why: pan out＝「（計画が）うまくいく」。今では3店舗、が結果。backed down（引き下がった）、dropped by（立ち寄った）、cut in（割り込んだ）は計画の結果を表さない。

questions.q: Sarah ____ a bad cold the day before her big presentation, so her colleague had to give it in her place.
choices: came up with
got away with
put up with
came down with
questions.why: come down with ～＝「（病気に）かかる」。同僚が代わりに発表した理由。came up with（思いついた）、got away with（うまく逃れた）、put up with（我慢した）は風邪と組まない。

questions.q: Even when the whole team argued that the deadline was unrealistic, the manager refused to ____ and insisted that the project be finished on time.
choices: lay off
back down
sum up
pass out
questions.why: back down＝「（主張を）引っ込める、折れる」。refused to と「期限通りにと言い張った」から、譲らなかった。lay off（解雇する）、sum up（要約する）、pass out（気を失う）は合わない。

questions.q: Researchers are still trying to ____ the exact reason why some seabirds return to the same nest year after year.
choices: pin down
wear out
run up
strike up
questions.why: pin down＝「（原因などを）突き止める」。理由をはっきりさせようとしている。wear out（すり減らす）、run up（（借金を）ためる）、strike up（（会話を）始める）は reason と組まない。

questions.q: The heavy snow ____ the delivery trucks for two days, so many stores in the area ran out of fresh vegetables.
choices: gave off
made up
turned in
held up
questions.why: hold up＝「遅らせる、足止めする」。トラックが来ず野菜が売り切れた。gave off（（においを）出した）、made up（作り上げた）、turned in（提出した）は合わない。

questions.q: After years of working long hours, Diana decided to ____ on her responsibilities at work so that she could spend more time with her children.
choices: cut back
cash in
look on
frown on
questions.why: cut back on ～＝「～を減らす」。子どもとの時間を増やすため仕事を減らす。cash in on（～につけ込む）、look on（傍観する）、frown on（～に眉をひそめる）は目的と合わない。

questions.q: The new puzzle app ____ quickly among teenagers, and within a month it had been downloaded more than a million times.
choices: fell apart
gave out
caught on
saw off
questions.why: catch on＝「流行する、人気が出る」。1か月で100万回以上ダウンロード、が根拠。fell apart（ばらばらになった）、gave out（尽きた）、saw off（見送った）は人気を表さない。

parts.title: 大問2 長文の語句空所補充
parts.desc: 約250語の説明文（3段落）の空所3つに入る語句を4つから選ぶ
parts.tip: 空所の前後1文ずつが根拠。In other words / As a result の後ろは前の内容のまとめ・結果になる。つなぎ語の空所は、前後が「逆接・追加・具体例・裏づけ」のどれかを先に決めてから選ぶ。
parts.intro: Read each passage and choose the best word or phrase from the four choices for each numbered blank.

sets.passage:
The Return of the Night Sky

For most of human history, people could look up on a clear night and see thousands of stars. Today, however, artificial lighting from streets, buildings, and advertisements has made the night sky far brighter than it would naturally be. In many large cities, residents can see fewer than twenty stars. This so-called light pollution is not just a problem for amateur astronomers. Studies suggest that it can disturb the sleep of people living nearby and confuse animals that rely on darkness, such as moths and migrating birds. In other words, excessive light ( 1 ).

In response, a number of towns have begun taking steps to reduce unnecessary lighting. The small town of Elmsworth, for example, replaced its streetlights with lamps that point downward and automatically dim after midnight. Officials were initially concerned that residents would feel unsafe walking home at night. ( 2 ), surveys conducted a year later found that most people had hardly noticed the change, and the town's electricity bill fell by nearly 40 percent.

Elmsworth's success has also brought unexpected benefits. Because its sky is now dark enough to see the Milky Way, the town has started attracting visitors who want to experience stargazing. Local hotels offer guided night-sky tours, and a nearby farm has opened a small observatory. Some experts believe that other communities could ( 3 ). If they are right, protecting darkness may turn out to be good not only for nature but also for business.

choices: affects far more than our view of the stars
is mainly a problem in rural areas
helps animals find food more easily
has become less common in recent years
questions.why: 直前で、睡眠の妨げや動物の混乱など、星が見えないこと以外の害が挙がっている。In other words でまとめるので「星の眺め以外にも影響する」。田舎の問題・動物を助ける・減っている、は本文と逆か無関係。

choices: For this reason
Similarly
In addition
As it turned out
questions.why: 前の文は「住民が不安になると心配した」、後ろは「ほとんど気づかなかった」。心配が外れた結果なので「結局のところ」。For this reason（このため）、Similarly（同様に）、In addition（さらに）は前後の食い違いを表せない。

choices: ignore the needs of local businesses
install brighter lights to attract tourists
turn their dark skies into a source of income
stop visitors from entering at night
questions.why: 前の文で星空ツアーや観測所が観光客を呼んでいる。最後の文の good for business につながるのは「暗い空を収入源にする」。明るい照明を増やす、は本文の主張と逆。

sets.passage:
Lessons from Ant Traffic

Anyone who has watched a line of ants carrying food back to their nest may have noticed something surprising: ants rarely seem to get stuck in traffic jams. Even when thousands of them use the same narrow trail, the flow continues smoothly. Human drivers, by contrast, often find themselves stopped on busy roads. This difference has led some scientists to study ants in the hope that they ( 1 ).

One reason ants avoid jams appears to be that they do not compete with one another. A driver may try to overtake other cars or change lanes to save a few seconds, which often forces those behind to brake suddenly. Ants, on the other hand, keep a steady pace and do not try to pass those in front of them. Researchers also found that when a trail becomes extremely crowded, ants ( 2 ). Rather than pushing forward, some simply wait at the nest until the trail clears, which prevents the situation from getting worse.

Engineers believe these findings could become useful as self-driving cars grow more common. Unlike human drivers, such vehicles could be programmed to share information and adjust their speed together, much like a colony of ants. ( 3 ), computer simulations based on ant behavior have shown that traffic could move up to 20 percent faster if all cars followed similar rules. Of course, human roads are far more complicated than ant trails, but nature may still offer valuable ideas for solving everyday problems.

choices: could be trained to carry heavier objects
would stop building nests near roads
might reveal ways to improve the movement of vehicles
may explain why drivers prefer large cars
questions.why: 直前で「アリは渋滞しないが人間の車はする」と比べている。研究の目的は車の流れを良くするヒントを得ること。重い物を運ぶ・巣の場所・大きな車の好みは渋滞と関係ない。

choices: reduce the number of individuals that set out
begin to move much more quickly
leave the trail to search for new food
start to compete for the best positions
questions.why: 続く文で「前に進まず巣で待つアリもいる」とある。つまり出発する数を減らす。速く動く・競う、は第2段落の内容と逆。

choices: Indeed
Nevertheless
Otherwise
Even so
questions.why: 前の文「車が協調できれば」を、後ろの文が「シミュレーションで最大20%速くなった」と裏づけている。だから「実際に」。Nevertheless / Even so（それでも）は逆接、Otherwise（さもなければ）は条件で、どれも合わない。

sets.passage:
Paying with Time

In most economies, people exchange goods and services for money. In recent decades, however, a different system known as "time banking" has spread to communities around the world. In a time bank, members earn credits by helping others, and one hour of work always earns one credit, no matter what the task is. A retired teacher who spends an hour tutoring a child earns exactly the same as someone who spends an hour repairing a fence. Members can then use their credits to receive help from others. Supporters say this system ( 1 ).

Time banks have proved particularly valuable for people who have skills but little money. At the Harlow Valley Time Bank, for example, many members are elderly residents who live alone. Some of them used to feel that they had nothing left to offer society. Through the time bank, however, they have found ways to share their knowledge, such as teaching cooking or knitting. As a result, many say that they ( 2 ). Organizers also report that members are more likely to know and trust their neighbors.

Despite these benefits, time banks face certain difficulties. Because no money is involved, they often depend on a single volunteer coordinator who matches members with tasks, and when that person leaves, the whole system can quickly fall apart. ( 3 ), some members are reluctant to ask for help, even when they have plenty of credits to spend. To overcome these challenges, some time banks now use simple smartphone apps that let members find each other directly.

choices: rewards those with professional qualifications
treats everyone's time as equally valuable
allows members to exchange credits for cash
was designed mainly for large businesses
questions.why: どんな仕事でも1時間＝1クレジットで、元教師も柵の修理も同じ。つまり全員の時間を同じ価値として扱う。資格のある人を優遇・現金に替える、は本文と逆。

choices: prefer to spend time on their own
have decided to move to the city
feel more connected to their community
earn more money than before
questions.why: 一人暮らしの高齢者が知識を分け合うようになった結果。次の文の「近所の人を知り信頼する」とも合う。一人で過ごしたい・都会へ引っ越す・収入が増える、は本文に無い（お金は使わない仕組み）。

choices: As a result
In addition
In contrast
For this reason

sets.passage:
Rediscovering Old Apples

A century ago, farmers in some regions grew hundreds of different varieties of apples. Each had its own flavor, color, and season, and many were suited to particular uses, such as baking, making juice, or storing through the winter. Today, however, most supermarkets sell only a handful of varieties. These were chosen mainly because they look attractive, travel well, and stay fresh for a long time on store shelves. As a result, many traditional varieties ( 1 ).

In recent years, a growing number of enthusiasts have set out to find and save these forgotten apples. Members of one group, the Ridgefield Orchard Society, search old farms and abandoned gardens for trees that may be the last of their kind. When they find one, they cut small branches from it and attach them to young trees, a technique that allows the variety to be reproduced exactly. The work is slow, however, because ( 2 ). Supporters argue that protecting rare varieties is more than just a hobby. Some old apples are naturally resistant to certain diseases, which could make them useful to scientists developing new varieties that require fewer chemicals. ( 3 ), many chefs and cider makers have become interested in their unusual flavors. The society now sells young trees to the public, hoping that more people will plant them in their own gardens.

sets.passage:
The Value of Boredom

For many people today, a moment of boredom is something to be eliminated as quickly as possible. While waiting for a bus or standing in line at a store, most of us automatically reach for our smartphones to check messages, read the news, or play a game. Psychologists have noted that, as a result, many people now go through entire days without ever experiencing the feeling of having nothing to do. Although this might seem like a harmless habit, some researchers believe that constantly avoiding boredom may come at a cost.

In one common type of experiment, participants are first asked to complete a dull task, such as sorting a large pile of beans by color for fifteen minutes. Afterward, they are given a creative challenge, like thinking of as many uses as possible for a pair of plastic cups. Compared with participants who skipped the dull task, those who had been bored tend to produce a greater number of ideas, and their ideas are often judged to be more original. One explanation is that boredom encourages the mind to wander. When the brain is not occupied by outside information, it begins to make unexpected connections between memories and thoughts, a process that can lead to creative solutions.

Boredom may also play a role in motivating people to change their lives. Because the feeling is unpleasant, it signals that a person's current activity is not meaningful or rewarding enough. In this sense, boredom works much like hunger: it pushes us to search for something better. People who feel bored at work, for example, may be inspired to learn a new skill or look for a more challenging position. Researchers warn, however, that this benefit depends on how people respond. Those who react to boredom by turning to quick sources of entertainment, such as scrolling endlessly through social media, may relieve the feeling temporarily without ever addressing its cause.

None of this means that boredom is always good. Long periods of boredom, particularly among teenagers, have been linked with poor concentration and unhealthy habits. Nevertheless, some educators now argue that children should be given more unstructured time, free from screens and scheduled activities. Rather than rushing to fill every quiet moment, they suggest, parents and teachers could allow children to discover for themselves how to turn boredom into something productive. Learning to tolerate a little boredom, it seems, may be a valuable skill in a world full of constant distractions.

questions.q: According to the passage, what is one finding of experiments on boredom?
choices: People who are easily bored find it difficult to complete simple tasks such as sorting beans.
Creative challenges become less interesting to people after they have used their smartphones.
People who have just performed a boring task often come up with more creative ideas.
People who avoid boredom are better at making connections between their memories.
questions.why: 第2段落：退屈な作業をした人のほうが、アイデアの数が多く独創的だった。豆の仕分けは実験の作業の例で、退屈しやすい人が苦手という話ではない。記憶をつなげるのは退屈した時の脳の働き。

questions.q: What does the author of the passage suggest about the way people respond to boredom?
choices: It is usually a sign that people are hungry or tired and need to take a rest.
People who feel bored at work should avoid changing their jobs too quickly.
Its benefits may be lost if people simply distract themselves with easy entertainment.
Using social media is an effective way to deal with the real cause of boredom.
questions.why: 第3段落の後半：SNS などすぐ手に入る娯楽に逃げると、一時的に気分は晴れても原因に向き合わない。hunger は「より良い物を探させる」たとえで、本当に空腹という意味ではない。

questions.q: Some educators believe that
choices: teenagers should spend longer periods alone in order to improve their concentration.
children may benefit from having free time without screens or planned activities.
schools should give children more structured activities to prevent them from feeling bored.
parents should fill their children's quiet moments with educational games.
questions.why: 第4段落：画面や予定の無い自由な時間を子どもに与えるべきだ、と主張する教育者がいる。長い退屈は10代の集中力低下と結びつくとあり、予定を詰める・静かな時間を埋める、は逆。

sets.passage:
Gardens on the Rooftops

In many cities around the world, rooftops are being transformed into gardens. These so-called green roofs are covered with a layer of soil and plants, ranging from simple grasses to small trees. Although the idea of growing plants on buildings is centuries old, it has attracted new attention as city governments search for ways to make urban areas more pleasant and environmentally friendly. In the city of Marston, for example, all new commercial buildings above a certain size must now include either a green roof or solar panels.

One major advantage of green roofs is their ability to manage rainwater. In ordinary cities, rain falls onto hard surfaces such as concrete and asphalt and flows rapidly into drains. During heavy rain, drainage systems can become overloaded, and water may collect on roads and sidewalks. A green roof, by contrast, absorbs much of the rain and releases it slowly over several hours. Some of the water is also taken up by the plants and returned to the air. Engineers in Marston estimate that the city's green roofs now hold back millions of liters of water each year that would otherwise have entered its crowded drains.

Green roofs can also help to cool both buildings and the surrounding area. Dark rooftops absorb heat from the sun, and in summer they can become hot enough to raise temperatures inside the building and in nearby streets. Plants, however, provide shade and release moisture, which keeps the roof surface much cooler. As a result, buildings with green roofs often need less air conditioning, which reduces energy costs. In addition, the gardens provide a home for insects and birds that would otherwise struggle to find food in the city.

Despite these benefits, green roofs are not suitable for every building. Soil soaked with water is extremely heavy, so older buildings may need to be strengthened before a roof garden can be added, which can be very expensive. Green roofs also require regular maintenance, such as removing weeds and checking that water is draining properly, and building owners are sometimes unwilling to pay for this. To encourage more people to install them, some cities offer financial support or reduce property taxes for owners who do so. Supporters believe that, as the costs of materials fall and more people become aware of the benefits, green roofs will become a common feature of city life.

questions.q: What is one way that green roofs help cities deal with rain?
choices: They slow down the speed at which rainwater reaches the drainage system.
They direct rainwater into large tanks so that it can later be used for drinking.
They prevent rain from ever falling onto concrete and asphalt surfaces.
They allow engineers to build smaller drains under the city's streets.
questions.why: 第2段落：雨を吸い込み、数時間かけてゆっくり放出する（releases it slowly）。だから排水管に一気に流れ込まない。飲み水のタンク・小さな排水管は本文に無い。

questions.q: According to the passage, green roofs can reduce energy costs because
choices: dark rooftops reflect the sun's heat away from the building.
the insects and birds living on the roof help to control temperatures.
they make it possible to install solar panels at a lower price.
the plants keep the roof cooler, so less air conditioning is needed.
questions.why: 第3段落：植物が日陰を作り水分を出すので屋根が涼しく、冷房が少なくて済む。黒い屋根は熱を吸収する（反射ではない）。鳥や虫は別の利点。

questions.q: What is one problem with installing green roofs?
choices: Cities have started to charge higher taxes to owners of buildings that have them.
Some buildings must be made stronger to support the weight of wet soil.
The plants used on green roofs often attract insects that damage buildings.
They cannot be combined with other systems such as solar panels.
questions.why: 第4段落：水を含んだ土はとても重く、古い建物は補強が必要で費用がかかる。税金はむしろ減らす市がある。太陽光パネルは「緑の屋根か太陽光パネル」の選択肢として出てくるだけ。

sets.passage:
Railways and the Birth of Standard Time

Today, it seems natural that everyone in the same region sets their clocks to the same time. For most of history, however, this was not the case. Before the nineteenth century, each town determined its own time based on the position of the sun. When the sun reached its highest point in the sky, it was noon. Because the sun appears to move from east to west, noon arrived a few minutes earlier in a town in the east than in one slightly to the west. For people who rarely traveled far from home, these small differences did not matter at all.

The arrival of the railway changed this situation dramatically. Trains allowed people to travel long distances in just a few hours, and suddenly the variety of local times became a serious problem. A railway company operating across a large area had to publish timetables, but which town's time should those timetables follow? Some companies used the local time of the city where their headquarters were located, while others listed several different times for each station. Passengers often missed trains because they were confused about which time was being used. More seriously, the confusion made it difficult to schedule trains safely on shared tracks.

To solve this problem, railway companies began to adopt standard times that applied across entire regions. Instead of hundreds of local times, a country could be divided into a small number of time zones, each covering a wide area. Within a zone, every clock would show the same time, and neighboring zones would usually differ by exactly one hour. At first, this was simply a business decision by the railways, and many towns continued to use their own local time for everyday purposes. Some residents resented being told to follow "railway time," feeling that it was unnatural to ignore the sun.

Over time, however, the convenience of standard time won people over. As telegraph networks expanded, businesses and governments found it increasingly useful for everyone to agree on the time. Eventually, time zones were made official by law in many countries, and they were coordinated internationally so that the whole world could be connected by a single system. The next time you check the time on your phone, it may be worth remembering that the familiar idea of a shared time was, in large part, created by the needs of the railways.

questions.q: Before the nineteenth century,
choices: each town set its clocks according to where the sun was.
towns in the east set their clocks later than towns in the west.
most people traveled long distances in order to compare local times.
noon was decided by a national organization in each country.
questions.why: 第1段落：町ごとに太陽の位置で時刻を決め、太陽が一番高い時が正午。東の町のほうが正午が早く来る（later ではない）。遠出する人は少なかった。

questions.q: What problem did railway companies face?
choices: Passengers refused to buy tickets unless timetables used their own local time.
Their headquarters were located too far from most of the stations they served.
Trains could not travel quickly enough to make long journeys practical.
The many different local times made it hard to create clear and safe schedules.
questions.why: 第2段落：どの町の時刻で時刻表を作るか決められず、乗客は混乱し、同じ線路での安全な運行も難しかった。本社の時刻を使った会社はあるが、距離が問題だったわけではない。

questions.q: What does the passage say about the introduction of standard time?
choices: It was not immediately accepted by everyone, but its usefulness gradually became clear.
It was first introduced by law and was later adopted by the railway companies.
Neighboring time zones were set several hours apart in order to avoid confusion.
Telegraph companies opposed it because it made their services less necessary.
questions.why: 第3・4段落：初めは反発する住民もいたが、電信の広がりとともに便利さが認められた。順番は鉄道会社が先で法律は後。隣の時間帯の差はふつう1時間。

sets.passage:
Learning from the Bottom Up

In most companies, mentoring follows a familiar pattern: an experienced senior employee offers advice and guidance to a younger colleague who is just beginning his or her career. In recent years, however, a growing number of organizations have started to experiment with the opposite arrangement. In so-called reverse mentoring programs, junior employees are paired with senior managers, and it is the younger employee who acts as the teacher.

The idea first became popular as a way to help senior staff keep up with new technology. Many executives built their careers before social media and smartphone apps became central to business, and some feel uncomfortable using them. A young employee who has grown up with these tools can explain not only how they work but also how customers of his or her generation actually use them. At Brightwell Insurance, a mid-sized firm, managers who took part in such a program said they had gained a far better understanding of why the company's online advertising was failing to reach younger customers.

Supporters argue, however, that the benefits go well beyond technical skills. In many organizations, junior employees rarely have the chance to speak directly with top managers, and their opinions may pass through several layers of supervisors before reaching the people who make decisions. Reverse mentoring creates a direct channel of communication. Senior managers can learn what younger staff think about issues such as working conditions and company culture, while junior employees gain confidence and a clearer view of how the business is run. Some companies have also found that employees who participate are less likely to quit, which can save considerable recruitment costs.

Nevertheless, reverse mentoring programs do not always succeed. Some senior managers find it difficult to accept advice from people much younger than themselves, and they may not take the sessions seriously. Junior employees, for their part, may hesitate to give honest feedback to someone who has power over their careers. Experts recommend that companies set clear goals for each pair and make it explicit that the sessions are confidential. They also suggest that the mentoring should go both ways, with each person sharing knowledge with the other. When these conditions are met, reverse mentoring can help to break down the barriers between generations in the workplace.

questions.q: Why did reverse mentoring first become popular?
choices: It allowed companies to train new employees without hiring outside experts.
Senior managers wanted to teach younger staff how to use social media for business.
Younger employees demanded more opportunities to be promoted to senior positions.
It offered a way for senior staff to learn about new technology from younger colleagues.
questions.why: 第2段落：上の世代が新しい技術についていくための方法として広まった。教えるのは若い社員の側なので、上司が SNS を教える、は逆。

questions.q: According to supporters, one benefit of reverse mentoring is that
choices: it reduces the number of supervisors that a company needs to employ.
it allows the opinions of junior staff to reach senior managers more directly.
it gives senior managers a chance to criticize younger employees' work.
it makes it easier for companies to recruit staff from other firms.
questions.why: 第3段落：若手の意見は何層もの上司を通るが、この制度は直接の連絡の道を作る。採用費が減るのは辞める人が減るからで、他社から人を取りやすくなるわけではない。

questions.q: What do experts recommend in order to make reverse mentoring programs successful?
choices: Allowing senior managers to choose which junior employees they work with.
Recording each session so that supervisors can check what was discussed.
Making sure that both people in each pair learn something from each other.
Limiting the program to employees who have worked at the company for many years.
questions.why: 第4段落：目標をはっきりさせ、内容は秘密にし、お互いに教え合う（go both ways）ようにする。秘密にするので、記録して上司が確認する、は逆。

sets.passage:
Rewilding the Farm

For centuries, the main goal of agriculture has been to control nature. Farmers clear land, remove plants they do not want, and manage animals carefully so that fields produce as much food as possible. In recent decades, however, some landowners have begun to experiment with a very different approach known as rewilding. Rather than managing every part of their land, they step back and allow natural processes to shape it, often by bringing back large grazing animals similar to those that once lived in the area.

One well-documented example is Holloway Estate, a former dairy farm of about 1,400 hectares. For many years, its owners struggled to make a profit. The soil was heavy clay, which made it difficult to grow crops, and the price of milk kept falling. Eventually, they decided to sell their dairy cows and machinery. In their place, they released small herds of hardy cattle, ponies, and pigs, and then largely left the land alone. Fences between fields were removed, and ditches that had been dug to drain water from the land were allowed to fill in.

The results surprised even the owners. Within a decade, thorny bushes had spread across former fields, providing shelter for young trees, which grew up through them while protected from the grazing animals. The pigs, by digging in the soil for roots, created patches of bare ground where new plants could take hold. As the landscape became more varied, wildlife returned in remarkable numbers. Several bird species that had become rare in the region began nesting on the estate, and surveys recorded a sharp increase in butterflies and other insects. Scientists who studied the estate concluded that the grazing animals played a key role: by eating some plants and trampling others, they prevented any single type of vegetation from taking over.

Rewilding has not been without its critics, though. Some neighboring farmers complained that the estate looked untidy and that weeds from its land were spreading into their fields. Others argued that, with the world's population still growing, it is irresponsible to take farmland out of food production. Supporters respond that land like Holloway's was never very productive in the first place, and that the estate still produces some food, since a limited number of animals are sold for meat each year. They also point out that the estate now earns money from sources that did not exist before, such as nature tours, camping, and payments from companies that want to fund environmental projects.

Perhaps the most important lesson from projects like Holloway is that rewilding does not have to be all or nothing. Few farmers are willing to give up their entire business, but many have started to adopt elements of the approach, such as leaving wide strips of wild plants along the edges of fields or allowing hedges to grow larger. Such changes can provide homes for wildlife while still allowing the main part of a farm to be used for crops. In this way, the ideas behind rewilding may spread far beyond the few estates that have adopted it completely.

questions.q: Why did the owners of Holloway Estate decide to change how they used their land?
choices: Scientists asked them to provide a home for rare birds and insects.
Neighboring farmers had complained about the noise from their machinery.
They had been offered payments by companies to stop producing milk.
Their dairy business was not making enough money, partly because of the poor soil.
questions.why: 第2段落：粘土質の土で作物が育ちにくく、牛乳の値段も下がり続けて利益が出なかった。企業からの支払いは、変えた後に生まれた新しい収入源（第4段落）。

questions.q: According to the passage, grazing animals helped the estate by
choices: eating the thorny bushes that had prevented young trees from growing.
digging ditches that removed water from the heavy clay soil.
stopping one kind of plant from spreading over the whole area.
keeping birds and insects away from the newly planted crops.
questions.why: 第3段落の最後：食べたり踏んだりして、1種類の植物が全体を覆うのを防いだ。とげのある茂みは若木を守る側。溝は埋まるに任せた。

choices: They admit that rewilding should only be carried out on highly productive farmland.
They argue that weeds from the estate actually benefit neighboring farms.
They claim that the world's population is no longer growing as quickly as before.
They say the estate still produces some food and has found new ways to earn income.

choices: Holloway Estate kept its fences so that its animals would not escape onto other farms.

The number of insects on Holloway Estate fell after the pigs were released.
Most farmers who learn about rewilding decide to give up growing crops completely.

sets.passage:
The Wisdom of Crowds

More than a century ago, visitors to a country fair were invited to guess the weight of a large ox. About eight hundred people took part, including farmers and butchers, but also many ordinary townspeople who knew little about animals. When a scientist later examined the guesses, he found that individual estimates varied widely, and few were close to the correct answer. The average of all the guesses, however, was almost exactly right, differing from the true weight by less than one percent.

This phenomenon, often called "the wisdom of crowds," has since been observed in many situations. When large groups of people estimate the number of coins in a jar, for example, the group's average is frequently more accurate than the estimates of almost all individual members. The explanation is fairly simple. Each person's guess contains some error, but some people guess too high and others too low. When many guesses are combined, these errors tend to cancel each other out, leaving an answer close to the truth.

However, researchers have found that crowds are only wise under certain conditions. The most important is independence: each person must make his or her own judgment without being influenced by others. In one experiment, participants answered questions about geography and population figures. Some groups answered alone, while others were shown what other members had guessed before making their own estimates. Surprisingly, the groups that could see one another's answers performed worse. Their guesses became more similar, which made participants feel more confident, but the average moved further from the correct answer. Because everyone had been influenced by the same early guesses, their errors no longer canceled out.

Diversity is another key factor. A group whose members all have the same background and sources of information is likely to make the same mistakes. A group that includes people with different experiences, by contrast, brings a wider range of knowledge to a problem. For this reason, some organizations now deliberately seek opinions from employees in many different departments when making forecasts, rather than relying only on a small team of specialists. One retail company, for instance, found that combining sales predictions from hundreds of store workers produced more accurate results than the forecasts prepared by its planning department.

These findings have important implications for how decisions are made. Meetings in which people discuss a problem openly may seem like a good way to combine knowledge, but they can actually reduce the independence of individual judgments, particularly when a senior person speaks first. Some researchers therefore recommend that members of a group write down their opinions privately before any discussion begins. Of course, the wisdom of crowds is not a perfect solution. For questions that require specialized knowledge, such as diagnosing a rare disease, a single expert may be far more reliable than a large group of non-experts. Still, when used carefully, the combined judgment of many people can be a surprisingly powerful tool.

questions.q: What did the scientist discover about the guesses made at the country fair?
choices: Although most individual guesses were wrong, their average was very accurate.
Farmers and butchers made much better guesses than ordinary townspeople did.
Most visitors guessed a weight that was close to the ox's true weight.
The average of the guesses was far higher than the real weight of the ox.
questions.why: 第1段落：1人ずつの推測はばらばらで正解に近い物は少ないが、平均は1%未満の差でほぼ正確だった。農家と町の人の比較はしていない。

questions.q: In the experiment described in the third paragraph, the groups that saw other members' answers
choices: produced more accurate estimates because they could correct one another's mistakes.
felt less confident because their guesses had become more varied.
became more confident even though their combined estimate became less accurate.
refused to change their original guesses after seeing the others' answers.
questions.why: 第3段落：他人の答えを見たグループは推測が似てきて自信は増したが、平均は正解から遠ざかった。推測は「ばらばら」ではなく「似てきた」。

questions.q: What does the author say about the retail company?
choices: Its planning department refused to share sales information with workers in its stores.
Its store workers all had similar backgrounds, so their forecasts were almost the same.
It decided to close its planning department and rely only on outside experts.
Predictions gathered from many store employees were better than those of its planning department.
questions.why: 第4段落：何百人もの店員の売上予測を合わせると、企画部の予測より正確だった。多様な人の意見を集める例で、同じ背景・外部の専門家だけ、は逆。

questions.q: Which of the following statements is true?
choices: Open discussions are the best way to make sure that individual judgments stay independent.
Asking people to record their views before a discussion may lead to better group decisions.
Large groups of non-experts are always more reliable than a single specialist.
The wisdom of crowds works best when a senior person shares an opinion first.
questions.why: 第5段落：話し合いの前に各自が意見を書き出すよう勧める研究者がいる。公開の話し合いや上の人が先に話すことは独立性を下げる。珍しい病気の診断などは専門家1人のほうが確か。

sets.passage:
Why Waiting Feels Long

Few people enjoy waiting in line, whether at a supermarket checkout, a bank, or an amusement park. Businesses have long understood that long waits can drive customers away, and many have invested heavily in reducing them. Researchers who study the psychology of waiting, however, have found that the actual length of a wait is often less important than how the wait feels. Two people who wait for exactly the same amount of time may have very different experiences, depending on the conditions around them.

One of the most consistent findings is that waiting with nothing to do feels longer than waiting while occupied. A frequently told story concerns an office building whose tenants complained constantly that the elevators were too slow. Rather than install expensive new elevators, the building's managers placed large mirrors beside the elevator doors. People waiting began looking at themselves and at others, and the complaints almost stopped, even though the elevators were just as slow as before. Similar thinking explains why many theme parks entertain visitors in line with videos or decorations, and why restaurants often hand menus to customers who are waiting for a table.

Uncertainty also makes waiting harder to bear. When people do not know how long they will have to wait, they tend to overestimate the time that has passed and become anxious. For this reason, many businesses now display estimated waiting times. Interestingly, some companies deliberately make these estimates longer than necessary. If customers are told they will wait twenty minutes but are seated after fifteen, they feel pleasantly surprised. Studies suggest that this small difference can significantly improve how customers rate their overall experience, even though they still waited for a considerable period.

Perhaps the strongest influence on how people feel about waiting is their sense of fairness. Customers become especially frustrated when they see someone who arrived after them being served first. This is one reason why many banks and post offices have switched from having a separate line for each counter to a single line that leads to all the counters. Although a single line may look longer and does not necessarily reduce the average waiting time, it guarantees that people are served in the order in which they arrived. Surveys show that customers generally prefer this system because no one can be unlucky enough to choose a slow line.

These insights have become increasingly valuable as businesses compete to provide a better customer experience. Some experts warn, however, that managing the psychology of waiting should not become a substitute for providing good service. Distracting customers or adjusting their expectations may make a short wait more pleasant, but it is unlikely to satisfy people who are kept waiting for an unreasonable length of time. Ultimately, these experts argue, businesses need to combine an understanding of human psychology with genuine efforts to serve their customers efficiently.

questions.q: The story about the office building shows that
choices: people complain less about waiting when they have something to occupy their attention.
installing faster elevators is the only way to reduce complaints from tenants.
people who are waiting for elevators prefer not to look at other people.
most complaints about elevators are caused by poor building design.
questions.why: 第2段落：鏡を置いたら、エレベーターの速さは同じなのに苦情がほぼ止まった。何かに気を取られていれば待ち時間は短く感じる、の例。新しいエレベーターは入れていない。

questions.q: Why do some companies give customers waiting-time estimates that are longer than necessary?
choices: It discourages customers from joining the line when the business is busy.
Being served earlier than expected makes customers feel more satisfied.
Customers tend to underestimate how long they have already been waiting.
It allows staff to take more breaks without customers noticing.
questions.why: 第3段落：20分と言われて15分で案内されると、うれしい驚きになり評価が上がる。人は待った時間を多めに感じる（overestimate）ので、underestimate は逆。

questions.q: What is one reason that banks have introduced single lines?
choices: They ensure that customers are served in the order they arrive.
They greatly reduce the average amount of time that customers have to wait.
They make the line look shorter, so customers are less likely to leave.
They allow customers to choose which counter they want to use.
questions.why: 第4段落：1列だと来た順に必ず呼ばれ、公平だと感じる。平均の待ち時間は必ずしも減らず、列はむしろ長く見える。

questions.q: Which of the following statements is true?
choices: Theme parks were the first businesses to use mirrors to entertain customers.
The actual length of a wait is the most important factor in how customers feel.
Some experts believe that psychological methods cannot make up for very long waits.
Customers prefer having a separate line for each counter because they can choose the fastest one.
questions.why: 第5段落：気をそらしたり期待を調整したりしても、長すぎる待ちに満足はしないと警告する専門家がいる。第1段落では実際の長さより感じ方が大事、とある。

In many rural areas, schools are facing a serious challenge. As the number of young people living in the countryside declines, some schools have only a handful of students in each grade, and it has become difficult to hire teachers for every subject. In response, a number of school districts have started connecting classrooms in different towns by video so that one teacher can teach students in several schools at the same time.

Supporters of this approach say it offers students opportunities they would not otherwise have. A small school that cannot afford a full-time physics or Chinese teacher can still offer these subjects by joining a class taught from a larger school elsewhere. Students also benefit from interacting with peers from other communities, which can expose them to a wider range of opinions and help them prepare for life at university or in the workplace. Furthermore, sharing teachers allows districts to use their limited budgets more efficiently.

However, the system has drawbacks as well. Teachers say it is much harder to notice when a student is confused or losing interest if that student is on a screen in another building. Practical subjects such as science experiments and music can be difficult to teach remotely, and problems with internet connections sometimes interrupt lessons. Some parents also worry that if more classes move online, local schools may eventually be closed altogether, which could weaken the sense of community in their towns. Experts therefore suggest that online classes should be combined with regular face-to-face visits from teachers.

Every year, large amounts of fruit and vegetables are thrown away before they ever reach a store. Much of this food is perfectly safe to eat, but it is rejected because it is the wrong size or shape, or because it has small marks on its skin. In recent years, however, some supermarkets have started selling such "imperfect" produce at lower prices, and several online companies now deliver boxes of it directly to customers' homes.

This trend has been welcomed for several reasons. Farmers benefit because they can earn money from crops that they would previously have had to throw away or sell very cheaply as animal feed. Consumers, meanwhile, can buy healthy food for less, which is especially helpful for families on tight budgets. Environmental groups also support the idea, pointing out that reducing food waste lowers the amount of land, water, and energy needed to produce food.

Nevertheless, selling imperfect produce has not been entirely straightforward. Some shoppers remain unwilling to buy fruit and vegetables that look unusual, even when they are cheaper, so stores sometimes end up throwing them away anyway. Critics have also raised concerns that if supermarkets sell cheaper produce, they may put pressure on farmers to lower the prices of their regular crops as well. In addition, some delivery services have been criticized for buying up produce that would otherwise have been donated to food banks. To address these issues, some companies now publish information about where their produce comes from and how much of it would otherwise have been wasted.

In the past, few companies would have allowed employees to bring their pets to work. Recently, however, a growing number of businesses, particularly technology firms and small design studios, have begun to welcome dogs in the office. Some companies allow dogs every day, while others set aside one day each week when employees can bring them along.

Companies that have adopted such policies report a number of benefits. Many employees say that having dogs around makes them feel more relaxed, and some studies have found that workers who interact with animals during the day report lower levels of stress. Dogs can also encourage people to talk with colleagues they might not otherwise speak to, which can improve teamwork. In addition, pet owners no longer need to worry about leaving their dogs alone at home for long hours, so they may be more willing to stay late when necessary. Some firms even advertise their pet-friendly policies in order to attract talented job applicants.

On the other hand, there are clear disadvantages. Some employees are allergic to dogs, and others are simply afraid of them, so they may feel uncomfortable or even unable to work in the office. Dogs can be noisy or cause damage to furniture and equipment, and disagreements can arise when a colleague's dog behaves badly. For these reasons, companies that allow dogs usually set strict rules, such as requiring dogs to be well trained and limiting them to certain areas of the building. Experts also advise businesses to consult all their employees before introducing such a policy.

Over the past two decades, many cities have launched programs to plant large numbers of trees along streets, in parks, and around schools. Some city governments have set ambitious goals, such as planting hundreds of thousands of trees within ten years, and they encourage residents to take part by offering free young trees to plant in their own gardens.

There are good reasons for this enthusiasm. Trees provide shade, which can lower temperatures on city streets during hot summers and reduce the need for air conditioning in nearby buildings. They also absorb some of the pollution produced by traffic and help to slow the flow of rainwater into drains. Moreover, research suggests that people who live in areas with more greenery tend to feel less stressed and are more likely to go outside and exercise, which may improve their health.

However, planting trees is only the first step, and some programs have struggled. Young trees need regular watering and care for several years, and in some cities a large percentage of newly planted trees have died because there was not enough money or staff to look after them. Tree roots can also damage sidewalks and underground pipes, which leads to costly repairs. In addition, critics point out that new trees are sometimes planted mainly in wealthier neighborhoods, while poorer areas, which often have the fewest trees, receive less attention. As a result, experts argue that cities should focus not only on how many trees they plant but also on where they plant them and how they will maintain them.

Traditionally, the only way to see the treasures held by a museum was to visit the building in person. In recent years, however, many museums have begun to photograph the objects in their collections and make the images available online free of charge. Some have even created virtual tours that allow users to explore their galleries from anywhere in the world.

These digital collections have brought a number of advantages. People who live far from major cities, or who cannot travel because of poor health or the cost involved, now have access to artworks and historical objects that they might never otherwise have seen. Teachers can use high-quality images in their lessons, and researchers can study items in detail without having to travel. In addition, most museums are able to display only a small fraction of what they own, so putting their collections online allows the public to see many objects that have been kept in storage for years.

Not everyone, however, is convinced that the trend is entirely positive. Photographing and recording thousands of objects is expensive and time-consuming, and some smaller museums worry that the money would be better spent on caring for the collections themselves. Some museum directors also fear that if people can see everything online, fewer of them will pay to visit in person, which could reduce an important source of income. Others point out that viewing an image on a screen cannot replace the experience of standing in front of an actual painting or sculpture. Many museums have therefore started using their online collections to encourage visits, for example by linking images to information about upcoming exhibitions.

In many countries, universities have traditionally been places for young people who have just finished high school. Recently, however, increasing numbers of people in their fifties, sixties, and even older have been enrolling in university courses. Some study part-time while continuing to work, while others return to education after retiring. To meet this demand, a number of universities have introduced special programs and reduced fees for older students.

There are several reasons for this trend. As people live longer and healthier lives, many want to use their later years to study subjects they did not have the chance to pursue when they were young. Others hope to gain new qualifications so that they can change careers or continue working for longer. Research also suggests that learning new things can help older people keep their minds active and avoid feeling isolated. Universities, meanwhile, benefit from a new source of students at a time when the number of young people is falling.

Nevertheless, older students can face difficulties. Many find it hard to adjust to new technology, such as online learning systems, and some feel out of place among classmates who are decades younger than they are. The cost of tuition can also be a burden for those living on a pension. In addition, some younger students have complained that their older classmates tend to dominate discussions in class. To address these challenges, some universities now offer introductory computer courses and organize events where students of different ages can get to know one another. Experts believe that such efforts will become increasingly important as societies continue to age.
